name: Esoteric Astrology — the Bailey school, paraphrased
description:
One school's teaching, paraphrased: the soul-centred ('esoteric') astrology set out in Alice A. Bailey's Esoteric Astrology (1951). These are our words, not the book's.

COPYRIGHT. The book is © 1951 Lucis Trust, renewed 1979, so it is under US copyright through 2046. Lucis Trust's terms do not allow its text to be stored in a database or retrieval system, or used to train AI, without written permission. This grammar therefore holds no sentence of the book: only our own paraphrase, plus the book's table of sign rulers (Tabulation VI, print p. 68) and the membership of its three crosses, given as facts with attribution. Read the book itself at the Lucis Trust online edition.

WHAT THE SCHOOL ADDS. Each sign has three rulers: the orthodox one most astrologers use, an esoteric one (the book's 'disciple' column) and a hierarchical one (the book assigns this column to what it calls the Creative Hierarchies; later writers often read it as the initiate's rulers, which the book does not say in the passages checked). Among the rulers are Vulcan, a planet astronomers looked for and never found, and the Earth itself; Pluto rules Pisces here, not Scorpio. The school pictures two directions round the wheel: the ordinary one runs backward through the signs (Aries, Pisces, Aquarius...), and the soul-centred one runs forward in the order textbooks use. It groups the signs into three crosses. Notes about planets 'veiled' by the Sun or the Moon come from scattered passages that disagree with one another, and each sign item labels them so.

HOW TO USE IT HERE. The school ranks people: it ties each ruler set to a kind of person. This library reports that as the school's own teaching and never applies it to a reader. You choose which ruler set to look through; nothing here assigns anyone a level. It is off by default in the schools filter (grammars/astrology-schools). Read the sky to know yourself, not to be told your fate: each item ends with a question, not a verdict.

Every sign, cross and Pluto item links to its item in grammars/the-structure-of-the-sky (metadata.source_deck / source_item_id). Vulcan and the Earth have no structure item.

metadata.cross_source: Alice A. Bailey, Esoteric Astrology (Lucis Publishing, 1951), the table of the three crosses, print p. 80

sections.What it is: The school groups the four cardinal signs as a cross and ties it to beginnings of the largest kind; the crisis it names for this cross is initiation. Other schools call the same four signs the cardinal modality. Signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn.
sections.How the school uses it (the record): The book ties each cross to a stage on its path, from ordinary experience (Mutable) through discipleship (Fixed) to initiation (Cardinal), and says the arms of the crosses will one day matter more than the houses in the soul's chart. This library gives that as the school's own teaching, never as a measure of anyone. Most charts have planets on more than one cross.
sections.An invitation: Where in your life does something new keep wanting to begin?

sections.What it is: The school groups the four fixed signs as a cross and ties it to turning round: the crisis it names here is reorientation, a change of direction held steadily. Other schools call the same four signs the fixed modality. Signs: Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius.
sections.How the school uses it (the record): The book ties each cross to a stage on its path, from ordinary experience (Mutable) through discipleship (Fixed) to initiation (Cardinal), and says the arms of the crosses will one day matter more than the houses in the soul's chart. This library gives that as the school's own teaching, never as a measure of anyone. Most charts have planets on more than one cross.
sections.An invitation: What are you holding steady, and what would it mean to turn it round?

sections.What it is: The school groups the four mutable signs as a cross and pictures it as the cross of changing experience, the crisis of coming into a life. Other schools call the same four signs the mutable modality. Signs: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces.
sections.How the school uses it (the record): The book ties each cross to a stage on its path, from ordinary experience (Mutable) through discipleship (Fixed) to initiation (Cardinal), and says the arms of the crosses will one day matter more than the houses in the soul's chart. This library gives that as the school's own teaching, never as a measure of anyone. Most charts have planets on more than one cross.

metadata.position_note: No position exists. This library never places Vulcan on a wheel and never uses a made-up ephemeris for it.
metadata.rulers_source: Alice A. Bailey, Esoteric Astrology (Lucis Publishing, 1951), Tabulation VI 'Planetary Rulers in 3 Tabulations', print p. 68
metadata.structure_link: none: the-structure-of-the-sky has no Vulcan item, because it holds only bodies that exist

sections.In this school (our paraphrase): Vulcan rules Taurus in the esoteric and the hierarchical columns. The book pictures it as a smith at the forge, working in the densest material, going down into the depths to shape something useful and beautiful: an energy that starts things and also breaks old forms. It links Vulcan closely with the Sun, sometimes hidden behind it, sometimes standing for it.
sections.In the sky: No such planet has been found. In 1859 the astronomer Urbain Le Verrier proposed a planet inside Mercury's orbit to explain an unexplained drift in Mercury's path. Claimed sightings were never confirmed, and general relativity (1915) explained the drift without it. Vulcan is a symbol with no position.
sections.How to look through it here: As a ruler only. Readers of this school sometimes look at Vulcan through the Sun (the link above) or through the Moon (another passage of the book). Some software offers a 20th-century hypothetical ephemeris for it; that is a guess, not an observation, and this library does not use it.
sections.An invitation: What in you works slowly out of sight, shaping something that is not ready to be seen yet?

sections.In this school (our paraphrase): The Earth rules Sagittarius in the esoteric column and Gemini in the hierarchical one. The book counts it among the planets it does not call sacred. Few other schools give the Earth a sign at all.
sections.In the sky: Real, and underfoot. A chart is drawn from the Earth, so the Earth has no place of its own on it; practitioners who use it put it exactly opposite the Sun. That is a convention, not an observation.
sections.An invitation: If the ground you stand on had something to say about where you are aiming, what would it say?

metadata.table_note: The table gives Scorpio to Mars; another passage names Pluto as Scorpio's ruler and calls Mars Pluto's other self (print p. 507). The book disagrees with itself here.

sections.In this school (our paraphrase): Most modern astrology gives Pluto to Scorpio. In this school's table Pluto rules Pisces, in the esoteric and the hierarchical columns, and Scorpio keeps Mars. The book is not consistent about it: another passage gives Pluto to Scorpio and calls Mars Pluto's other self.
sections.Reading it: Many schools read Pluto as endings and renewal. Set beside Pisces, the last sign of the wheel, this could mean the close of a cycle. It could also mean a sensitivity that has been through something and come out changed. What does it mean to you?
sections.An invitation: What is ending for you, and what might it be clearing room for?
